study_identification.title: Individual-level deviations from normative brain morphology in violence, psychosis, and psychopathy

study_characteristics.study_objective: To assess the potential of normative modeling in forensic psychiatry neuroimaging research by investigating individual patterns of deviations from the norm in persons with a history of severe violence and schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD-V), non-violent persons with schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD-NV), persons with a history of severe violence without schizophrenia spectrum disorder (nonSSD-V), and healthy controls (HC).

dataset_name.answer: Pre-trained normative model reference cohort from braincharts (58,836 individuals from 82 sites); Local calibration cohort (TOP; STROKEMRI; uTOP; sTOP)

hc_n.answer: 998 (calibration set); 196 (matched healthy controls used in analysis)

hc_age.answer: Calibration set n=998: age range not specified; Matched HC n=196: mean 31.9 (SD 10.0, min 15.7, max 70.9)

hc_sex.answer: Calibration set n=998: F 608 (60.9%), M 390 (39.1%); Matched HC n=196: all male (100%)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v7.1; Destrieux atlas for cortical parcellation; probabilistic atlas for subcortical volume segmentation; MRIqc for quality checking

quality_checking_detail.answer: Two-step quality control: (1) All T1w images processed using MRIqc pipeline; (2) Two trained raters (NT and JR) visually examined scans marked for exclusion by MRIqc. Visual evaluation of lateral and medial snapshots of all cortical maps; individuals removed if surface values had negative values, unusual patterns, or significant value imbalance across hemispheres. Total exclusions: 52 males and 20 females due to insufficient T1w image quality, and 3 additional male individuals due to spurious abnormal brain findings.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Pre-trained normative models from braincharts account for site/scanner effects. An additional harmonization step was implemented using an unmatched group of healthy controls (n=998) to fine-tune model parameters, enabling the application of normative models to unseen sites. Scanner was included as an independent variable in the normative models along with age.

model_origin_detail.answer: Pre-trained normative models from https://github.com/predictive-clinical-neuroscience/braincharts. Models were trained using data from 58,836 individuals aged 2-100 from 82 sites. See Rutherford et al. (2022), eLife, 11:e72904 for details.

modeling_method.answer: Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping using sinarcsinsh function

response_variable.answer: Cortical thickness (148 Destrieux regions); Cortical area (150 regions); Subcortical volumes (32 structures)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and Scanner were modeled in the pre-trained normative models. Specific fixed/random effect specification not detailed in the paper, but models use Bayesian linear regression framework.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study uses pre-trained normative models that account for age and scanner effects. An additional harmonization step with n=998 healthy controls was used to fine-tune model parameters for unseen sites. However, the paper does not provide detailed validation metrics (e.g., explained variance, MSLL, skewness, kurtosis) to demonstrate how well nuisance structure is handled. The models use Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping, which can model mean and variance, but the paper lacks explicit validation of whether site effects, variance differences, and other nuisance factors are appropriately captured.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To account for the absence of scanner data used to acquire data in the model, an additional harmonization step was implemented. An unmatched group of healthy controls (n = 998) was utilized to fine-tune model parameters, enabling the application of normative models to unseen sites. [...] To model non-linear effects accurately, normative models were trained using Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping using sinarcsinsh function. The dependent variable was set to the ROI values of volume, area, or thickness, while the independent variables were age and scanner.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The paper does not report validation metrics (e.g., explained variance, MSLL, correlation, skewness, kurtosis) on the training data or any non-independent subset of the training data. The focus is on applying pre-trained models to new clinical data rather than validating model performance on the training dataset.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: No explicit validation on training data is reported in the paper.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study uses a calibration set of n=998 healthy controls to fine-tune model parameters for their local data. This represents a form of adaptation/validation on independent data within the same domain (healthy controls), but no explicit validation metrics are reported for this calibration step. It is unclear whether this calibration set was used purely for adaptation or whether validation metrics were computed.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: An unmatched group of healthy controls (n = 998) was utilized to fine-tune model parameters, enabling the application of normative models to unseen sites.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The normative models, which were pre-trained on 58,836 individuals from 82 sites, are applied to a different domain consisting of clinical groups (SSD-V, SSD-NV, nonSSD-V) and local healthy controls from Norwegian cohorts (TOP, STROKEMRI, uTOP, sTOP). The paper reports extensive analyses of deviation patterns, group comparisons, and associations with clinical variables, demonstrating validation of the normative models in a different clinical and geographical domain. However, formal validation metrics (e.g., predictive accuracy, calibration metrics) are not reported; instead, the focus is on clinical interpretability of deviation scores.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: We used pretrained normative models from https://github.com/predictive-clinical-neuroscience/braincharts. Briefly, models were trained using data of 58835 individuals aged 2-100 from 82 sites. [...] Participants (n = 782 male/608 female) were recruited from the Oslo area as part of four studies: the Thematically Organized Psychosis study (TOP), the STROKEMRI study, The Youth-TOP study (uTOP), and The Forensic Psychiatry study (sTOP). [...] The remaining participants consisted of four groups: (1) persons with a history of severe violence and comorbid schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD-V, n = 38), (2) persons with a history of severe violence and no comorbid psychosis disorder (nonSSD-V, n = 20), (3) persons with no history of violence but with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD-NV n = 138), and (4) healthy controls (HC, n = 196).

clinical_dataset.answer: TOP (Thematically Organized Psychosis study); STROKEMRI; uTOP (Youth-TOP study); sTOP (Forensic Psychiatry study)

diseases_studied.answer: Schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD) with history of violence; Schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD) without history of violence; History of severe violence without schizophrenia spectrum disorder

clinical_groups_age.answer: SSD-V: mean 34.7 (SD 8.9, min 19.2, max 54.1); SSD-NV: mean 29.0 (SD 8.7, min 15.1, max 57.8); nonSSD-V: mean 42.4 (SD 14.4, min 9.2, max 71.0)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score; extreme deviations defined as |Z| > 2; percentage of individuals with extreme positive (Z > 2) and negative (Z < -2) deviations at each ROI; total count of extreme deviations per individual

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Case-control group difference testing on deviation scores using matched healthy controls (1:1 ratio, matched by age and scanning site) via matchIt package. General linear models (GLM) implemented in PALM toolkit with permutations, controlling for age effects and including ICV for volume/area analyses. Family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons (number of ROIs, three modalities, 8 contrasts). Cohen's d effect sizes computed. Permutation tests to compare frequency of extreme deviations between groups. GLM with 10,000 permutations in PALM to examine associations between PCL-R scores and deviation scores, adjusting for age, psychosis status, and ICV. Main findings: SSD-V showed significantly higher mean z-score values than HC for negative deviations in right subcallosal area (pmc-fwe=0.020, t=4.5, d=1.17) and left medial occipito-temporal and lingual sulcus thickness (pc-fwe=0.022, t=4.3, d=0.99). SSD-NV exhibited significantly larger positive deviations in left inferior lateral ventricle volume (pc-fwe=0.0085, t=4.2, d=0.61) and pallidum volume (pc-fwe=0.025, t=4.0, d=0.57) compared to HC. Frequency of positive deviations differed significantly between SSD-V and HC (p=0.0190, d=0.58), and frequency of negative deviations differed between SSD-NV and HC (p=0.0086, d=0.31). No significant associations found between PCL-R scores and brain morphology deviations after correction for multiple comparisons, though trend-level positive associations were observed in right subparietal sulcus area (d=1.8, punc=0.0041) and parieto-inferior supramarginal gyral thickness (d=1.8, punc=0.0056).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Heterogeneous patterns of individual deviations from normative brain morphology were found in persons with violence and/or psychosis, with SSD-V showing most prominent deviations in collateral transverse sulcus, lingual gyrus, and cerebellum regions, differing from SSD-NV and nonSSD-V.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study found overall heterogeneous patterns of brain deviations on the individual level across all clinical groups. SSD-V displayed extreme negative deviations in 2.6% of cortical area regions and 2.1% of subcortical regions (3-5 fold increase vs. HC at 0.6%). The highest proportions of extreme negative deviations in SSD-V were found in left anterior (13.2%) and right posterior (10.5%) segments of collateral transverse sulcus area, medial area of left lingual gyrus (10.5%), and right cerebellar cortex volume (10.5%). SSD-NV showed highest deviations in right hemisphere's parieto-occipital and suborbital sulcus areas (7.2% each). NonSSD-V showed highest deviations in left paracentral lobule and sulcus, and middle frontal sulcus (20% and 15% respectively). Overall, 89.5% of SSD-V and 65% of nonSSD-V had at least one extreme deviation, though no single region exceeded 13.2% (SSD-V) or 20% (nonSSD-V). Statistical analyses revealed SSD-V had significantly higher negative deviations than HC in right subcallosal area (pmc-fwe=0.020, d=1.17) and left medial occipito-temporal/lingual sulcus thickness (pc-fwe=0.022, d=0.99). SSD-NV showed significantly larger positive deviations in left inferior lateral ventricle (pc-fwe=0.0085, d=0.61) and pallidum volume (pc-fwe=0.025, d=0.57) vs. HC. No significant associations were found between psychopathy traits (PCL-R) and deviation patterns after correction for multiple comparisons.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Relatively small sample sizes, particularly for violence groups (SSD-V n=38, nonSSD-V n=20); male-only sample limits generalizability; use of atlas-defined ROI parcellations may have lower representation of true associations compared to vertex-wise analyses; models not corrected for substance use which could affect brain morphology; did not control for cumulative effects of antipsychotic medication; most severely ill or aggressive persons were not eligible due to consent/safety concerns; violence defined as lifetime binary variable which is narrower than WHO definition; cross-sectional design cannot distinguish between disease mechanisms and effects of early-life influences/developmental trajectories; cross-sectional normative modeling has shown lower individual-level prediction propensity than longitudinal models.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Study demonstrates feasibility of normative modeling in forensic psychiatry populations with small sample sizes. The heterogeneous individual patterns differed from traditional case-control group-level findings, illustrating that normative modeling captures variance without 'failing' to replicate earlier studies. Findings point toward brain regions involved in visual processing, object recognition, emotional processing, and cerebellar function as potentially relevant to violence in psychosis context. Authors suggest these individual-level deviations may ultimately provide clinicians with neurobiological information that, together with other clinical parameters, could inform targeted treatment and violence prevention interventions. The low regional overlap between nonSSD-V and SSD-V (consistent with general heterogeneity findings in schizophrenia) reflects diverse underlying factors contributing to violence.

general_notes.general_notes: This study applies pre-trained normative models (braincharts from Rutherford et al. 2022) to a forensic psychiatry population, demonstrating the utility of normative modeling in small, specialized clinical samples. The calibration cohort of n=998 healthy controls included both males and females, while the analysis focused on male-only samples due to the nature of the forensic population. The study included participants from four Norwegian studies: TOP (Thematically Organized Psychosis), STROKEMRI, uTOP (Youth-TOP), and sTOP (Forensic Psychiatry study). Two GE 3T scanners were used: GE Signa HDxt with 8-channel head coil (FSPGR sequence) and DiscoveryMR750 with 32-channel head coil (BRAVO sequence). All participants were male in the final analysis groups, reflecting the predominance of men in forensic psychiatry populations. Violence was defined as court or hospital record verified episode of severe violence: homicide, attempted homicide, or physical (including sexual) violence toward other persons. The SSD-V group had DSM-IV diagnosis of schizophrenia spectrum disorder (schizophrenia n=35, schizoaffective n=1, schizophreniform n=1, other psychosis n=1) and were in high security hospital wards. The nonSSD-V group had no psychosis disorder and all were in high security prison serving preventive detention sentences. Clinical assessments included SCID-I (age ≥18), KIDDIE-SADS (age <18), PANSS for symptoms, WASI for IQ, AUDIT/DUDIT for substance use, and PCL-R for psychopathy traits. The paper references Rutherford et al. (2022) eLife 11:e72904 as the source of the pre-trained normative models and Bethlehem et al. (2022) Nature 604:525-33 for additional context on brain charts.
